EXTRA CLASS · KITCHEN HELPER

Welcome to the Kitchen.

The busiest room in the house, card by card: the everyday things a three-year-old already uses, the helper tools a four- or five-year-old can start with, the grown-up tools older kids love to name and the chef’s knife that teaches the kitchen’s biggest rule — knives are for grown-ups. Every lesson below is step by step, right on this page.

HOW THIS CLASS WORKS

Little cooks, real tools, one big rule.

The Kitchen is a bonus class, kept beside the main learning path: the regular classes stay the core sequence, and this one is for families with a small cook at the counter. Thirty-five cards name the busiest room in the house, and every step-by-step lesson is right here — the tool, the job it does, the words to say and one thing to try at the real counter.

Every card carries an age pill, and the pills are the pacing: Ages 3 and up for the everyday things kids already use — the spoon, the fork, the plate, the mug, the bowl, the fridge; Ages 4–5 for the helper tools — the whisk, the rolling pin, the ladle, the measuring cups, the oven mitt; Ages 6 and up for the grown-up tools kids this age don’t use yet but love to name — the garlic press, the box grater, the mortar and pestle; and one card that is grown-ups only, the chef’s knife, which stays on the wall to teach the kitchen’s biggest rule. Nothing needs to be rushed — the pills do the pacing.

THE CLASS GAME

Kitchen Helper.

The class game is three steps: the child finds the item — in the drawer, on the counter, in the picture pile; says its name — out loud, proud, with the whole kitchen listening; then sorts the cards into two piles: I can use it and Grown-ups only. Every child’s piles are a little different, and the arguments are the best part — a four-year-old who claims the whisk but hands over the grater has just run the whole safety curriculum in one sitting.

Sorting by hand leads to sorting for real: the hot-check (which cards get HOT? drop a toy oven mitt on each — the kettle, the saucepan, the frying pan, the baking tray), the sharp check (peeler, grater, blender blades — grown-up tools, sharp and careful), and the mine pile that grows a real little cook. The card names the tool; the kitchen uses the tool; the recipe does the rest.

THE KITCHEN’S RULES, SAID OUT LOUD

Knives are for grown-ups. Hot means don’t touch.

Two rules live in this class, and they are taught out loud, kindly and often. Knives are for grown-ups — the chef’s knife stays on the card because hiding sharp things makes them fascinating, while naming them makes them understood; the child’s own tools are real: the butter knife, the board, the banana to slice. Hot means don’t touch — the kettle, the saucepan, the frying pan and the baking tray are the hot family, and every one of their lessons teaches the same sentence: hot, don’t touch, grown-ups only, step back. The rules are said every time, which is exactly how they stick.

And because rules without jobs get tested, every safety rule here comes with a job: the safety checker who announces the boiling kettle, the beep-watcher who calls the microwave, the safety caller who calls the sizzle. Small hands stay busy; the hot and sharp stay where they belong.

Age ranges are a guide, not a test. Follow the pills, follow the recipe, follow the child — and keep the two rules louder than all of it: knives are for grown-ups, hot means don’t touch.

WHERE THE FOOD COMES FROM

Visit the Cafeteria.

The Kitchen class names the tools — and the school’s Cafeteria room names what those tools make: sixty-two food cards for ages 2–5, from the apple to the yogurt cup, each with its own pointing, counting or matching activity. The knife chops, the tray serves, and every food on the tray has a short page, a full lesson and a printable twin. Tools here, lunch there — the two rooms finish each other.

TEACHER’S LESSON

How this class is taught.

By the end of this class: your child has met all 35 cards in Kitchen Things, said each word with you and tried one small activity from the lesson.

  1. 01
    Welcome

    “Hello! Today we are learning about Kitchen Things. We have 35 cards, and we will look at them one at a time.”

    How: Sit side by side with the cards in front of you. Keep your voice warm and unhurried, and let your child touch the cards.

  2. Cards 1–10
  3. 02
    Card 1 · Baking Tray

    “Baking tray! The cookie tray. Dough balls go on the tray… spaced apart… into the oven it slides. And when it comes out — HOT! The tray is a hot one — grown-ups lift it, mitts go on, we never touch.”

    How: Your child’s job is the arranging: dough balls spaced on the tray (they spread — "give each cookie room for its neighbour"), then the tray goes to the oven by the grown-up. When the DING comes, watch the oven-mitt parade — tray out, onto the rack — and repeat the rule: "the tray is hot; we wait." Waiting is the job; cookies are the prize.

  4. 03
    Card 2 · Blender

    “Blender! The whirring machine. Fruit and milk go in the jug… lid on TIGHT… press the button — WHIRRR! Everything spins into a smoothie. The blades inside are SHARP — grown-ups handle the jug. We listen, we watch, we drink the smoothie!”

    How: Name it and run the ritual from a safe step away: fruit in (by you both), lid on tight (the grown-up’s click), button pressed by the grown-up — and your child is the smoothie announcer: "WHIRRR! It’s spinning!" Pour, drink, declare it the best smoothie yet. The blades stay a fact, not a fear: sharp things, grown-up hands, lid always on.

  5. 04
    Card 3 · Box Grater

    “Box grater! The four-sided tower. The cheese rubs up and down the big holes… SHRED — little cheese ribbons! Careful: the holes are SHARP. Look with your eyes, not your fingers.”

    How: This is a name-and-watch card: find the grater, count its four sides, notice the different hole sizes (big shreds, small shreds, slices). Then watch a grown-up grate cheese — palm flat on top, fingers far away — and say the sharp-things rule together: "sharp things are grown-up things." The cheese on pasta afterwards tastes like a science demo.

  6. 05
    Card 4 · Chef’s Knife

    “Chef’s knife! The big, sharp knife. This is the kitchen’s most important rule: KNIVES ARE FOR GROWN-UPS. Not today, not with help — grown-ups only. Your jobs are the butter knife, the spoon, the whisk. The chef’s knife waits for big hands, years from now.”

    How: Say the rule at the drawer, at the counter, at every chopping session — the same words, until the child says them first: "knives are for grown-ups." Give the sharp respect without the fear: the knife is a great tool that stays in the grown-up zone. Then point at the child’s own tools — the butter knife, the board, the banana to slice — so helping never stops, it just uses the right tools.

  7. 06
    Card 5 · Coffee Maker

    “Coffee maker! The morning machine. Water goes in the top, coffee in the filter… drip, drip, drip — the jug fills up! The jug and the plate stay HOT. We never touch the coffee maker — grown-ups pour.”

    How: Name it on the counter and watch a brew from the outside: water in, filter in, button on — drip drip drip. Say the rule while it drips: "the jug is hot; grown-ups only." Then the best part — your child can pour the COLD drinks instead: juice for the table, water for the cups. Everyone has a pouring job; the coffee maker’s job just belongs to the grown-ups.

  8. 07
    Card 6 · Colander

    “Colander! The bowl with holes. In go the grapes… water on… woooosh — the water runs through the holes and the grapes stay in! The colander drains the water away.”

    How: Wash fruit together: grapes or berries in the colander, your child works the tap, watches the water through the holes and shakes the bowl gently to dry. Then the grand demo — draining pasta (grown-up carries the hot pot, your child holds the colander steady in the sink). Holes that hold food and lose water: kitchen physics, visible.

  9. 08
    Card 7 · Cooking Spoon

    “Cooking spoon! The big wooden spoon. Hold it like this… stir, stir, stir the batter. Round and round — you are the stirrer today!”

    How: Fill a bowl with dry oats, hand over the spoon and let your child stir to their heart’s content — stirring dry is zero mess and all practice. Then promote the spoon to a real job: pancake batter, cake mix, scrambled eggs. The stir is the toddler’s signature on the meal.

  10. 09
    Card 8 · Cutting Board

    “Cutting board! The wooden board for chopping. The food goes ON the board — never chop without the board! Your banana goes here, your butter knife does the cutting… safe and steady.”

    How: Set up the board with a banana and a butter knife (the kid-safe kind): slice the banana into coins for cereal or a snack. The board stays still, the butter knife cuts soft food, the fingers stay clear. Then upgrade to soft strawberries or cheese cubes. Chopping is the proudest kitchen job there is — the board is what makes it safe.

  11. 10
    Card 9 · Dishwasher

    “Dishwasher! The machine that washes the dishes. In go the plates… the cups… the spoons. Click, the door shuts — whoosh, wash wash wash! Then everything comes out clean and warm.”

    How: Give your child the cutlery basket: spoons in spoon-side-up (or down — pick your family’s rule and keep it), one at a time, into their spots. Sorting silverware is matching practice that ends with a machine full of clean dishes. Unloading the cups to the low shelf is the promotion, saved for when the loading is expert.

  12. 11
    Card 10 · Food Thermometer

    “Food thermometer! The temperature checker. The pointy end goes IN the food… the screen shows a number — how hot the inside is! When the number is high enough, the food is properly cooked. Science you can eat!”

    How: Name it and watch it work: a grown-up checks a roast or a pot of soup, your child reads the number on the screen. Ask: "is the number big enough? Is the food ready?" It is a fine what-is-this demo — and it plants the big idea early: cooks check the inside, not just the outside. Numbers that keep people safe.

  13. Cards 11–20
  14. 12
    Card 11 · Fork

    “Fork! The pointy fork has four little teeth. Hold it in your fist… push it into the food… lift… and EAT! You did it with a fork!”

    How: Practise on the easiest wins first: banana coins, soft-cooked potato, melon cubes. Show the push-and-lift, then let the wobbly spearing happen — every skewered piece is a victory lap. Knife-and-fork teamwork comes later; today the fork does the whole show.

  15. 13
    Card 12 · Frying Pan

    “Frying pan! Sizzle sizzle — the pan is cooking! The pan gets VERY hot, and the oil jumps. We never touch the frying pan — grown-ups only. You crack the eggs at the counter, and the pan does the sizzling.”

    How: Split the job: your child cracks and whisks the eggs at the counter (the real, proud-making work), while the grown-up works the hot pan. When the sizzle starts, run the safety call — "sizzling means step back!" — and let your child declare it. The sizzle becomes the sound of a rule working.

  16. 14
    Card 13 · Funnel

    “Funnel! The little cone helper. Stand it in the bottle mouth… pour — the liquid runs down the funnel, right into the bottle! No spills, no puddles. The funnel makes every pour neat.”

    How: Name it and try it with supervision: funnel in an empty bottle, and your child pours water from a jug — watch it glide through, zero mess. Then the reverse question: what happens with NO funnel? (A puddle. A glorious puddle, outside, where puddles are allowed.) Cause and effect, demonstrated pour-ably.

  17. 15
    Card 14 · Garlic Press

    “Garlic press! The squeezer machine. A clove of garlic goes in the little basket… SQUEEZE both handles… and out comes tiny garlic through the holes! Smelly, strong and delicious.”

    How: This one is a name-it card: find the garlic press in the drawer, open and close the handles, maybe squeeze a clove with a grown-up’s hands on top. Smell the garlic after — the press’s whole party trick. Tools like this one are answered "that’s a garlic press — you’ll use one someday," which is exactly how future cooks are made.

  18. 16
    Card 15 · Kettle

    “Kettle! The kettle boils the water. The kettle gets VERY hot — hot, hot, hot! We look at the kettle… we never touch the kettle. Only grown-ups use the kettle. Hands behind your back — safety pose!”

    How: Teach the safety pose: hands clasped behind the back, one big step back from the stove whenever the kettle is on. Say the rule the same way every time — "hot, don’t touch; grown-ups only" — and let your child be the safety checker who announces "the kettle is HOT!" when the steam starts. Rules said with a job attached are rules children keep.

  19. 17
    Card 16 · Kitchen Timer

    “Kitchen timer! Turn the dial to the number… tick, tick, tick… and — DING! The timer says when. Twelve minutes for the cookies — set the timer, and when it dings, the cookies are done!”

    How: Hand the dial job over: your child sets the timer for cookies, for a ten-minute tidy-up, for "five more minutes of playground at home" (a carpet picnic). Watching the dial shrink makes time visible — and the DING is a celebration every single time. The timer turns waiting into a countdown game with a bell.

  20. 18
    Card 17 · Ladle

    “Ladle! The big deep spoon. Dip it in the soup… scoop… lift… pour into the bowl — there! One bowl of soup, served with care. Your turn to serve everyone!”

    How: Practise the scoop-pour with COLD soup or water in the sink first — dip, fill, carry, pour, no drips. Then promote it: ladling real (warm, not hot) soup into bowls at dinner, one bowl per person, counting them out. Serving the family is a big-kid job, and everyone says thank you.

  21. 19
    Card 18 · Measuring Cup

    “Measuring cup! The clear jug with the lines. Pour the milk in… stop at the line! The lines say how much. One cup of milk, exactly — that is measuring!”

    How: Set the jug on a level surface, crouch to eye level with the lines and pour slowly — milk creeping up to the line is surprisingly thrilling. Ask: "did we reach the line? A little more… STOP!" Then the measured milk goes into the real recipe. Numbers on a jug make the maths of baking visible and edible.

  22. 20
    Card 19 · Measuring Spoons

    “Measuring spoons! The little scoops on a ring — big, medium, small, tiny. One spoon of sugar… level it flat with a finger… in it goes. Small spoons, exact amounts!”

    How: Let your child be the spoon-keeper: find the size the recipe asks for, scoop, level it flat by dragging a finger across the top, tip it in. Leveling is the secret skill — heaped spoons and level spoons bake differently. Five little scoops later, the cake knows the difference.

  23. 21
    Card 20 · Microwave

    “Microwave! The magic heating box. In goes the plate… beep beep… the food comes out WARM. The microwave is a grown-up machine — we watch, we wait for the beep, we never touch the plate. Hot, hot!”

    How: Teach the beep-and-wait ritual: food in (by a grown-up), buttons pressed (by a grown-up), then your child is the beep-watcher whose job is to announce "BEEP! It’s ready!" The job satisfies the curiosity, keeps small hands off the controls and makes the waiting part of the game. Steam comes out when the door opens — one more step back.

  24. Cards 21–30
  25. 22
    Card 21 · Mixing Bowl

    “Mixing bowl! The big, big bowl. The flour goes in… the milk goes in… all in the mixing bowl. Now we stir! The bowl holds everything — no spills!”

    How: Set up the bowl on a damp cloth (it will not slide), and let your child be the pourer: cups of flour in, spoons of sugar in, cracks on the rim — the bowl catches everything. Naming it "the mixing bowl" gives the job an address, and jobs with addresses get done happily.

  26. 23
    Card 22 · Mortar and Pestle

    “Mortar and pestle! The stone bowl and the grinding club. Seeds go in the bowl… grind, grind, grind in circles… the seeds become powder. People have used these since long, long ago!”

    How: Name it, hold it, feel the weight — then watch a grown-up grind a few peppercorns or dried herbs and smell the difference: fresh-ground smells like the plant woke up. Try grinding a pinch of (safe, clean) rice with a grown-up’s hand guiding — heavy, slow, satisfying. Ancient tool, brand-new smell.

  27. 24
    Card 23 · Mug

    “Mug! The big cup with a handle. Two hands around the mug… careful… sip. Mugs are for warm drinks — cocoa, warm milk. Yum, just like the grown-ups!”

    How: Serve a child-size mug of warm (never hot) cocoa and teach the carry: two hands, walk slowly, set it down before you sip. The handle grip and the walking-with-liquid control are genuine skills — and being allowed a real mug tastes better than any drink.

  28. 25
    Card 24 · Oven Mitt

    “Oven mitt! The thick, puffy glove. The mitt stops the heat — hot tray? No problem, the mitt says! Grown-ups wear the mitt for the hot things… and look — it fits your hand too, for the cool trays.”

    How: Wear the mitts for a puppet show first — mitts say hello, mitts give a high-five — so the glove is a friend before it is equipment. Then the real lesson: the mitt goes on BEFORE touching anything that was in the oven, and the grown-up’s hand goes under the child’s for anything properly hot. Mitt on, both hands, slow walk — the oven-to-counter parade.

  29. 26
    Card 25 · Peeler

    “Peeler! The skin remover. It slides down the carrot… swish — long ribbons of skin fall off! The blade is sharp and hidden, so we LOOK with our eyes. Grown-ups peel; kids watch the ribbons fall.”

    How: Name it, find it in the drawer, open and close the blade gently (grown-up fingers on the blade end). Then watch the peeling demo — the ribbons are the show — and collect them for the compost or a soup pot. The rule comes with it: the peeler’s edge is sharp even when it looks tiny, so it is a grown-up tool until hands grow bigger and steadier.

  30. 27
    Card 26 · Plate

    “Plate! Here is your plate. One plate for you, one for me… set them on the table. The plate waits for the food. Yum!”

    How: Make plate-setting the child’s job: one plate per seat, handed out with ceremony — "Daddy’s plate… Grandma’s plate… YOUR plate." Counting the seats and matching the plates is early maths at dinner speed. Then the empty plate to the sink finishes the job.

  31. 28
    Card 27 · Refrigerator

    “Refrigerator! The big, cold fridge. The milk lives in the fridge… the yogurt, the apples, the cheese. Brrr — the fridge keeps our food cold and fresh. Close the door so the cold stays in!”

    How: Play fridge find-it: "bring me the milk… find the cheese… where do the eggs live?" Each trip teaches both the word and the food’s home. Then the door rule: one open, one close — the fridge works best when it is shut. A child who knows where food lives is a child who can help with every meal.

  32. 29
    Card 28 · Rolling Pin

    “Rolling pin! Hold both handles… push — roll, roll, roll! The dough gets flat and thin. Roll it this way, roll it that way… even all over. Ready for the cookie cutters!”

    How: Flour the counter, divide the dough and let your child roll their own piece flat — two hands, long pushes, edge to edge. Then cut cookies and compare shapes. A flat, even sheet is a real skill with a real score: the cookies themselves. Uneven cookies taste exactly the same, which keeps the joy safe.

  33. 30
    Card 29 · Saucepan

    “Saucepan! The pot that cooks the soup. The saucepan sits on the stove and gets VERY hot — hot, hot, hot! We never touch the saucepan. Grown-ups stir the pot; we stir our pretend pot over here.”

    How: Give the saucepan rule its own voice every time it is on the stove — "the pot is hot, step back" — then offer the safe twin: a toy pot at the play table where your child cooks the same meal with a wooden spoon. The pretend pot takes the real pot’s temptation away, and the rule does the rest.

  34. 31
    Card 30 · Spatula

    “Spatula! The flat flipper. Slide it under the pancake… lift… and FLIP! Over it goes. The spatula turns food over so both sides cook. Sizzle… flip… sizzle!”

    How: Practise the flip on a COLD pan with a piece of bread or a foam pancake — slide, lift, turn, no panic. Then hand the spatula over for the real flip (grown-up’s hand hovering, pan off the heat for the moment). One successful pancake flip is a breakfast legend that gets retold for years.

  35. Cards 31–35
  36. 32
    Card 31 · Strainer

    “Strainer! The net with the handle. The mesh is tiny — it catches the flour lumps, the seeds, the bits… and lets the liquid run through clean. Sift, strain, drip drip. The strainer is the careful one!”

    How: Name it next to the colander — same idea, finer net — and test the pair: which catches flour? Which catches pasta? Then watch a grown-up dust a cake with icing sugar through the strainer: a snowfall of sugar, all from the mesh. The strainer’s magic is its smallness — holes too small to see, big enough to matter.

  37. 33
    Card 32 · Toaster

    “Toaster! Bread goes in the slots… press the lever down — CLUNK! It gets warm and… POP! Toast jumps up! Only bread goes in the toaster — never fingers, never forks. Grown-ups help with the toast.”

    How: Let your child drop the bread in (with a grown-up beside them) and be the lever-presser — CLUNK is a deeply satisfying sound. When the POP comes, the grown-up lifts the toast out. The rule is said every time, same words: bread in, toast out, no fingers, no forks.

  38. 34
    Card 33 · Tongs

    “Tongs! The grabber arms. Squeeze to open… let go to grab! Pick up the pom-pom… squeeze… carry… drop in the bowl. Tongs are fingers that live on a stick!”

    How: Set up the tong relay: pom-poms or cotton balls moved from one bowl to another, one squeeze at a time. Then the real job — serving salad at dinner or picking up marshmallows for cocoa, tongs-only, no fingers allowed. The squeeze-and-carry grip is the exact muscle pattern pencils ask for later.

  39. 35
    Card 34 · Trash Bin

    “Trash bin! The wrapper goes in the bin. Step on the pedal… the lid opens… in it goes — whoosh! All tidy. The bin keeps our kitchen clean.”

    How: Make your child the bin chief for a day: every wrapper, every peel, every scrap goes in by THEIR pedal-and-toss. Then hand them the kitchen’s easiest real chore — emptying the little scraps bowl after dinner. Pedal, toss, close. Two-year-olds can do it; five-year-olds do it without being asked.

  40. 36
    Card 35 · Whisk

    “Whisk! The bouncy wire whisk. Hold the handle… whisk whisk whisk — fast circles! Look, the eggs have bubbles! The whisk makes fluffy eggs and fluffy cream.”

    How: Crack three eggs into the mixing bowl, hand over the whisk and time the whipping — can you make bubbles in thirty seconds? Wrist circles are hard work and enormously satisfying. The whisked eggs go straight into scrambled eggs, and the cook who whisked them eats prouder every time.

  41. 37
    Practice

    “Now you are the teacher! Pick any card and tell me what it is.”

    How: Let your child choose the card and say the word in their own way. Teaching someone else is the strongest way to remember.

  42. 38
    Check

    “Can you find Baking Tray? Now show me Measuring Cup.”

    How: A point, a fetch or the word all count as a pass. If they are unsure, name it for them and try again another day — there are no scores and no pressure.

  43. 39
    Well done

    “Well done! Today we met 35 cards. Let us look for one of them at home.”

    How: End on a win, then spot one of the words in real life today. Meeting it again in the real world is what makes it stay.

Read the script while you show the cards — the say-lines are yours to say out loud and the how-lines are the activity behind each step. Skip, shorten or repeat anything: the class bends to your child, never the other way round.
